description: We are a team of friends with a Computer Science background, participating in our first hackathon. Despite our busy schedules and individual commitments, we have come together to collaborate, share ideas, and build something over the weekend.
summary:
Field Shift is a web app that helps dryland wheat farmers in Finney County, Kansas compare crop rotations using NASA Earth observations. A farmer clicks their field, picks their top three priorities and the kind of year they expect, and sees three rotations side by side, their current wheat and fallow, wheat with sorghum and fallow, and wheat with a forage crop. Each card shows expected crop health with an honest uncertainty range, water need, bare soil days, erosion risk, why it was suggested, evidence from real fields, risks and data gaps.

We combined NASA POWER weather, MODIS greenness, SMAP soil moisture and SRTM elevation with USDA crop maps, soil survey and yields for 1,000 fields over 13 years. Our model separates the effect of each year’s rain and heat from the effect of each rotation. On years it never saw, it beat a fair baseline, and its range held the true value 80% of the time.

This matters because wheat and fallow leaves soil bare about 161 days a year and still fails in drought. In 2022 rain fell to 166 mm and yields halved. Field Shift makes the trade offs clear and leaves the decision to the farmer.
details:
What it does and how it works

Field Shift is a web app that helps dryland wheat farmers in Finney County, Kansas compare crop rotations. A farmer clicks their field on a map and answers six quick questions, their current rotation, rain fed or irrigated, soil type (prefilled from USDA soil data), their top three priorities, and whether to plan for a normal, dry or hot year. The app compares three rotations, wheat and fallow (the current practice), wheat with sorghum and fallow, and wheat with a forage crop. Each card shows expected crop health with an uncertainty range, water need, bare soil days, erosion risk, a score weighted by the farmer's priorities, a confidence level, a 12 month cover calendar, and the reasons, evidence, risks and data gaps behind it.

Behind the app, we built a dataset of 1,000 real dryland wheat fields over 13 years. USDA crop maps tell us which crop grew on each field every year. NASA MODIS greenness (NDVI) measures crop health, NASA POWER gives rain, heat and crop water demand, NASA SMAP gives soil moisture at planting and NASA SRTM gives elevation. The model splits crop health into a year effect, driven by rain and heat, and a rotation effect, measured by comparing each rotation with the county average in the same year so weather is held equal. A Monte Carlo step turns this into an honest range, and a sourced crop table (FAO 56, USDA AMS, Kansas State) adds water, income and feed scores.

Benefits

Farmers see trade offs instead of a single answer, for example that the sorghum rotation keeps wheat healthier and leaves soil bare about a month less each year, but needs more water. Every number comes from data, and missing data is shown as a gap, never guessed.

Intended impact

Help farmers and extension agents talk about rotations that cut bare soil and erosion and hold up better in drought. In 2022, rain fell to 166 mm and county wheat yield halved. In our data, wheat after sorghum stayed above average in dry years while wheat after fallow fell further. The method uses global NASA data, so it can be adapted to other regions such as Punjab.

Tools and technology

Python (pandas, NumPy, rasterio, scikit learn, pyet, LightGBM and SHAP for testing), FastAPI for the API, HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet and Chart.js for the web app, Google Earth Engine for MODIS, SMAP and SRTM, the NASA POWER API, the USDA CropScape service, Soil Data Access API and NASS QuickStats, pytest, Docker, Render and GitHub. We used Cursor and Claude to help write code and documents; the team reviewed all data choices and results. No special hardware, only our laptops.

Why it is creative

Instead of textbook rules, Field Shift learns rotation effects from 13 years of real field histories, and compares rotations within the same year to cancel out weather. It measures how each rotation behaves in dry years. It is honest about uncertainty, shrinks effects that rest on few fields, and never recommends an option it is not confident about.

Factors we considered

Fair testing, so we hid each year and tested on it, and compared against a fair baseline. We also tested a LightGBM model, and because it did not beat the simpler one, we shipped the simpler one. We removed mixed satellite pixels with a purity filter, focused on dryland fields, and kept the farmer form short and in plain language. We show our limits openly, one weather point per county, 250 m pixels, only six years of published yields, and few forage examples, and the tool supports, never replaces, the farmer and local agronomists.
